topics.title: Kinetic theory and the molecular nature of matter

learn.hook: You can't see air molecules, yet the pressure in your bicycle tyre is just billions of them drumming on the rubber every second.
points: Kinetic theory explains the behaviour of gases from the motion of their molecules: a gas is a swarm of rapidly moving molecules, and pressure and temperature come from that motion. Boyle, Newton, Maxwell and Boltzmann helped build it.
Atomic hypothesis: matter is made of tiny particles. Kanada in ancient India and Democritus in ancient Greece proposed indivisible constituents of matter.
Dalton's atomic theory explained the laws of definite and multiple proportions in chemistry.
Gay-Lussac's law: gases combine in simple ratios by volume. Avogadro's law: equal volumes of all gases at the same temperature and pressure contain equal numbers of molecules.

example.q: 2 L of hydrogen combine with 1 L of oxygen to give 2 L of water vapour (same T and P). How does Avogadro's law explain this?
steps: Equal volumes contain equal numbers of molecules.
So 2 molecules of H₂ react with 1 molecule of O₂ to give 2 molecules of H₂O.
The simple volume ratio 2 : 1 : 2 reflects the molecular ratio.

learn.reallife: The Vaisheshika school of ancient Indian philosophy, associated with Kanada, described matter as made of 'paramanu', tiny eternal particles.

topics.title: Molecular spacing and the ideal gas equation

learn.hook: One mole of water is about 18 mL as a liquid, but over 30 litres as steam at 100 °C. Molecules in gases are far apart.
points: In solids, atoms are tightly packed (~2 Å apart); in liquids slightly farther; in gases the spacing is about ten times larger and interactions are weak.

Atoms are always in motion. In a liquid–vapour system in a closed container, molecules leave and return at equal rates: dynamic equilibrium. A molecule in a gas travels a certain average distance between collisions (the mean free path).
Ideal gas equation: PV = μRT = Nk_BT, where μ = number of moles, N = number of molecules, R = 8.314 J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹ and k_B = R/N_A = 1.38 × 10⁻²³ J K⁻¹.
Avogadro's number N_A = 6.02 × 10²³ mol⁻¹. At STP (273 K, 1 atm), 1 mole of any gas occupies about 22.4 L.

example.q: How many molecules are there in 11.2 L of a gas at STP?

learn.reallife: LPG cylinders in Indian kitchens hold gas as a compressed liquid; when released it expands hugely because gas molecules are far apart.

topics.title: Gas laws, real gases and partial pressures

learn.hook: A scuba diver's tank holds a mix of gases, and each gas contributes its own share of the pressure. That's Dalton's law.
points: Boyle's law (PV constant at fixed T and μ) and Charles' law (V ∝ T at fixed P and μ) are special cases of PV = μRT.
Real gases follow the ideal gas law closely only at low pressures and high temperatures (molecules far apart, weak interactions).
Dalton's law of partial pressures: in a mixture of ideal gases, P = P₁ + P₂ + …, where each partial pressure Pᵢ = μᵢRT/V is the pressure that gas would exert alone.
Molecular volume fraction: in water vapour at 100 °C (ρ ≈ 0.6 kg m⁻³), molecules take up only ρ_vapour/ρ_liquid ≈ 0.6/1000 = 6 × 10⁻⁴ of the volume.

learn.hook: Picture a cricket ball hitting a wall again and again. A gas is that, with trillions of tiny balls every microsecond.
points: Assumptions: molecules are point-like (negligible size), move randomly, collide elastically with each other and the walls, and exert no forces except during collisions.
A molecule of mass m with velocity component vₓ hitting a wall transfers momentum 2mvₓ. Counting the molecules that hit in time Δt gives P = n m vₓ² (average).
Isotropy: random motion means vₓ² = v_y² = v_z² = v²/3 (averages), so P = (1/3) n m v̄², where n = number density and v̄² is the mean of the squared speed.
Pressure is the same in all directions (Pascal's law) because molecular motion is random.
Mixture: each gas contributes (1/3)nᵢm v̄ᵢ², so the total pressure is the sum of partial pressures (Dalton's law).

topics.title: Temperature, kinetic energy and rms speed

learn.hook: Oxygen molecules in the air of your classroom zip around at nearly 500 m s⁻¹, faster than a passenger jet!
points: From P = (1/3)nmv̄² and PV = Nk_BT: average translational KE per molecule = ½m v̄² = (3/2)k_BT. Temperature is a measure of average molecular kinetic energy.
Total translational KE E of a gas: PV = (2/3)E.
Root mean square speed: v_rms = √(v̄²) = √(3k_BT/m) = √(3RT/M), M = molar mass in kg mol⁻¹.
At the same temperature, lighter molecules move faster: v_rms ∝ 1/√M. E.g. v_rms(H₂) = 4 × v_rms(O₂).
Isotope separation: ²³⁵UF₆ and ²³⁸UF₆ have rms speeds in the ratio √(352/349) ≈ 1.0043; the slight difference in diffusion rates is used to enrich uranium.

example.q: Find the rms speed of oxygen molecules at 300 K (M = 0.032 kg mol⁻¹, R = 8.31 J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹).

learn.reallife: The nuclear fuel cycle at India's atomic facilities depends on uranium enrichment, which exploits tiny differences in molecular speeds of isotopes.

topics.title: Degrees of freedom and equipartition of energy

learn.hook: A helium atom can only zip around; an oxygen molecule can also tumble. Every extra way to store energy changes how much heat a gas needs.
points: Degrees of freedom: independent ways a molecule can have energy. Translational (3 for motion along x, y, z), rotational, vibrational.
Monatomic molecule (He, Ar): 3 translational degrees of freedom. Rigid diatomic molecule (O₂, N₂): 3 translational + 2 rotational = 5.
A vibrational mode has both kinetic and potential energy, so it contributes two quadratic terms (2 × ½k_BT = k_BT).

Law of equipartition of energy: in thermal equilibrium, each quadratic energy term (each translational and rotational degree of freedom, and each of the two terms of a vibrational mode) has average energy ½k_BT per molecule.

example.q: Find the average energy of a rigid diatomic molecule at temperature T, and the energy of 1 mol.

learn.reallife: Nitrogen and oxygen, which make up most of the air we breathe in Delhi or Kochi, behave as rigid diatomic gases at room temperature.

topics.title: Specific heats of gases from equipartition

learn.hook: Measured C_v for helium is 12.5 J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹ and for nitrogen about 20.8. Equipartition predicts both numbers almost perfectly.
points: Rigid diatomic: U = (5/2)RT, C_v = (5/2)R, C_p = (7/2)R, γ = 7/5 = 1.4. With vibration also active: C_v = (7/2)R, C_p = (9/2)R, γ = 9/7.
Polyatomic (3 translational, 3 rotational, f vibrational modes): C_v = (3 + f)R, C_p = (4 + f)R, γ = (4 + f)/(3 + f).
Predicted values agree well with measurements for monatomic and many diatomic gases at room temperature (e.g. He ≈ 12.5, N₂ ≈ 20.8 J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹).

example.q: Find C_v, C_p and γ for a rigid diatomic gas (R = 8.31 J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹).
steps: C_p = C_v + R = (7/2)R = 29.09 J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹.

learn.reallife: The γ of air (≈ 1.4), used by engineers designing jet engines and wind tunnels, comes straight from the diatomic nature of N₂ and O₂.

topics.title: Specific heat of solids and gas mixtures

learn.hook: At room temperature most solids need about 25 J to warm one mole by 1 K, but near absolute zero that number plunges. Classical physics can't explain why.
points: Solids: each atom oscillates in 3 dimensions. Each direction has KE and PE terms: 2 × ½k_BT per direction, so 3k_BT per atom.
Hence U = 3RT per mole and C = 3R ≈ 25 J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹ (Dulong–Petit law). At constant pressure and volume the values are nearly equal for solids.
At low temperatures, specific heats of solids (and the vibrational part for gases) fall below classical values. Explaining this needs quantum ideas (energy comes in discrete amounts).
Gas mixtures: C_v(mix) = (μ₁C_v1 + μ₂C_v2)/(μ₁ + μ₂). Heat for a gas in a cylinder: Q = μC_vΔT (rigid) or μC_pΔT (constant pressure).

example.q: Find C_v of a mixture of 1 mol of helium and 1 mol of oxygen (rigid).

learn.reallife: Cryogenic engines developed by ISRO handle materials near very low temperatures, where specific heats are far below the room-temperature 3R values.

learn.hook: Gas molecules move at hundreds of metres per second, yet a smell takes minutes to cross a room. They keep bumping into each other.
points: Mean free path l: the average distance a molecule travels between successive collisions.
l = 1/(√2 n π d²), where n is the number density and d the molecular diameter.
l decreases if the gas is denser (larger n) or the molecules are bigger (larger d). l ∝ 1/n, so at constant T, l ∝ 1/P.
Collision frequency ≈ v̄/l; time between collisions ≈ l/v̄. For air at STP, l ≈ 10⁻⁷ m, much larger than the molecular size (~10⁻¹⁰ m) and than the spacing (~3 × 10⁻⁹ m).
Typical estimates: average spacing (1/n)^(1/3), mean free path, and rms speed at a given temperature.

example.q: Molecules of diameter d = 2 × 10⁻¹⁰ m have number density n = 2 × 10²⁵ m⁻³. Estimate the mean free path (π ≈ 3.14, √2 ≈ 1.414).

learn.reallife: Vacuum chambers at ISRO's test facilities pump air down so far that the mean free path becomes metres long, mimicking space conditions for satellites.

quiz.q: The mean free path of gas molecules is
options: The total distance in one second
The average distance travelled between successive collisions
The distance to the container wall

quiz.q: If the number density of a gas is doubled, its mean free path becomes
quiz.mistake: Thinks more molecules mean longer free paths

quiz.q: If the molecular diameter is halved (same n), the mean free path becomes how many times?
The formula for mean free path is
quiz.explain: Inverse of collision cross-section times density (with √2 for relative motion).

At constant temperature, if the pressure of a gas is reduced to one-tenth, the mean free path becomes how many times the original?
Why does a smell spread slowly across a room even though molecules move fast?
options: Smell molecules are too heavy to move
Molecules collide very frequently and keep changing direction
quiz.explain: The short mean free path makes the motion a random walk.

quiz.q:
Assertion (A): The mean free path in a gas decreases when the gas is compressed at constant temperature.
Reason (R): Compression at constant temperature increases the average speed of the molecules.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
quiz.explain: A is true because n increases. R is false: at constant temperature the average speed is unchanged.

teach.ask: Gappu asks why it takes a while to smell agarbatti from across a room when molecules zoom at hundreds of m/s. Explain mean free path.
teach.praise: Molecules crash into each other every ~10⁻⁷ m, so their path zigzags. That's the mean free path!
teach.nudge: What is the mean free path? How does it change with density and molecular size?
